title: Is a 30% success fee for R&D tax credits too high?
description: A 30% R&D tax credit fee sits at the top of published fee ranges; it is not unlawful as such, but audit-defense terms decide its value.

body.text: Is a 30% R&D tax credit fee too high? For US businesses claiming the federal credit, a 30% success fee sits at the top of every published fee range and can far exceed the $7,500 to $50,000 cost of a study, especially on large claims. It is not unlawful as such, but audit-defense terms decide its value.

This report is general information about United States federal tax rules and market practice. It is not legal or tax advice, and readers should obtain advice on their own facts from a qualified CPA, Enrolled Agent or tax attorney.
1. Summary

Conclusion (analysis): A 30% success fee sits at the top of every published fee range located, and because a percentage fee scales with the size of the credit rather than with the work required to prepare and defend it, a 30% fee can far exceed the cost of preparing a claim, particularly on large or well-documented claims.

Whether 30% is "too high" for a given business is ultimately a commercial judgment rather than a legal one. Contingent fees for ordinary refund claims are not prohibited by Circular 230 after Ridgely v. Lew, so a 30% fee is not unlawful as such, subject to the general bar on unconscionable fees. The facts below show how to test the fee: compare it to (a) the published fee ranges, (b) the realistic cost of the work, and (c) what the fee does and does not include if the claim is examined by the IRS or a state revenue department.
2. The credit the fee is charged against

As currently published by the Legal Information Institute at Cornell Law School, §41(a)(1) sets the core (regular) credit at 20 percent of the excess, if any, of the qualified research expenses for the taxable year over the base amount. A success fee quoted as a percentage is therefore a percentage of a credit that is itself a percentage of incremental qualified research expenses, which is why the dollar fee can move sharply with relatively small changes in the expenses claimed.
2.1 The "Four-Part Test"

§41(d)(1) defines qualified research as research (A) with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures, (B) undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature and the application of which is intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component, and (C) substantially all of the activities of which constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose (relating to function, performance, reliability or quality). The fourth element of the conventional "Four-Part Test" is the first one listed above: the expenditures must qualify under the research expenditure provision cross-referenced in §41(d)(1)(A).

Correction / currency note: The current statutory text of §41(d)(1)(A) cross-references section 174A and refers to "domestic research or experimental expenditures." The editorial notes to the statute attribute this change to Pub. L. 119-21 (enacted in 2025); the prior text referred to "specified research or experimental expenditures" under section 174. Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(2)(i) has not been updated and still refers to expenditures that may be treated as expenses under section 174 (with a cross-reference to Treas. Reg. §1.174-2). Where the statute and the regulation differ, the statute governs.

Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(5)(i) defines a process of experimentation as a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. The same paragraph adds that uncertainty about the appropriate design of a business component does not by itself mean that every activity undertaken to achieve that component is a process of experimentation.

Added detail: The "substantially all" element of §41(d)(1)(C) is quantified in Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(6). It is met only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. The test is applied separately to each business component, and the remaining activities must still satisfy §41(d)(1)(A) and must not be excluded under §41(d)(4). This 80 percent threshold is directly relevant to the fee question: a provider paid a percentage of the credit has an incentive to treat borderline activities as part of a process of experimentation, and the 80 percent rule is one of the points an examiner tests.
2.2 Ineligible general and administrative costs

Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(3) states that direct support of research activities does not include general administrative services or other services only indirectly of benefit to research activities. Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(b)(1), which governs supplies and personal property used in the conduct of qualified research, states that expenditures for supplies or for the use of personal property that are indirect research expenditures or general and administrative expenses do not qualify as in-house research expenses. Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(b)(2)(i) adds that utility costs such as heat, light and power for the research building are treated as general and administrative expenses.
3. Where 30% sits in the market

body.text: The source names the platform (Tax Cloud) and states that it charges 5% of tax savings up to £200,000 and 2.5% on savings above that amount (Myriad Associates, 2025 cost article). This is a UK pricing example. The same article puts UK fixed-fee services at £5,000 to £15,000 and software platforms from around £2,750.

The Myriad Associates comparison table (September 25, 2025) rates accountancy-practice claim quality as "Low-Medium" with a client time input of 6 or more hours, and rates online portals at a client time input of 10 or more hours, compared with 4 to 6 hours for boutique firms. The article's text adds that accountancy quality depends on whether the practice treats R&D as a specialist service or a side service, and that some practices outsource the technical work.

Analysis: On every published range located, 30% is the ceiling, not the midpoint. No US-specific market survey of §41 contingency rates was located, so the claim should be read as indicative rather than as a measured US benchmark. The one US source located (Acena Consulting) mentions roughly 30% only as a ceiling on hourly billing expressed as a share of the credit, which is consistent with 30% being treated as an upper bound rather than a standard rate.
3.2 Fee versus effort

Myriad Associates explains that percentage fees require no upfront payment and are based on the benefit obtained rather than the work involved, so that a simple £100,000 claim and a complex £100,000 claim can cost the same fee. The same article contrasts this with fixed fees, which it describes as rewarding efficiency.

On the cost of the work, Acena Consulting's US guide states that the base cost of a research credit study can range from about $7,500 to $50,000. The guide identifies the number of projects as the largest single component of the base cost, with project complexity, the number of people involved and other tax issues also driving cost, and notes that mid-market companies with revenue above $250 million may see higher fees. It states that internal use software projects take substantially more time to document than other projects. The guide describes audit defense as typically the largest add-on, which some firms bundle into their fee and which can add 15% to 100% to the cost; other listed add-ons include travel ($500 to $5,000 if a technical team works onsite), documentation systems (about $50 per user per month to $5,000 or more) and quarterly reviews (about $1,000 to $3,000 per quarter). The better reading is that the $7,500 to $50,000 base range does not include audit defense, which is priced separately or bundled at an added cost.

Internal use software is also subject to a statutory exclusion in §41(d)(4)(E): except to the extent provided in regulations, research with respect to computer software developed by or for the benefit of the taxpayer primarily for internal use is excluded, unless the software is used in qualified research or in a production process that otherwise qualifies. This exclusion and the regulatory exceptions to it explain much of the added documentation burden noted by Acena Consulting.

4. Conflict of interest and compliance risk
4.1 The incentive problem

Hull & Knarr (US) states that providers paid a percentage of the credits they identify may include non-qualified expenses that are not defensible, so the provider earns more while the client's credit faces more risk under audit. Brown Rudnick (UK, August 18, 2025) reports that many UK R&D advisers charged a share of the tax savings, which incentivized aggressive claiming, and describes claims for non-qualifying projects, inflated or misclassified costs, and assurances that HMRC would not check the claim. It also reports that claims were submitted for projects that did not meet the legal definition of R&D, and that HMRC has since tightened its rules, including adviser naming requirements and more compliance checks. These are professional commentary, not findings of a court or tax authority about the US market.

Qualification on Hull & Knarr: The same Hull & Knarr article states that a provider paid on a contingency fee is "precluded" by Circular 230 from protecting the client under audit as part of its R&D credit services, so that defending the work requires an additional fee. That legal characterization is not accurate as a general statement of current law. 31 CFR §10.27(b)(2) expressly permits a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with the IRS's examination of, or challenge to, an original return, and the rule does not bar a practitioner from defending work it prepared. The article's practical point, that audit defense may be billed separately and reduce the net benefit, stands as commentary; its legal premise should not be relied on.
4.2 How contingency fees are regulated in the US

ForrestBrown (UK, last updated June 30, 2026, originally published July 22, 2020) states that R&D tax credit advice is only partially regulated, leaving the industry prone to unscrupulous providers. ForrestBrown describes fee structures (percentage-based "no win, no fee," fixed fees, time and materials, upfront fees and restricted success fees) but gives no specific percentages.

For the US, the relevant rule is Circular 230, 31 CFR §10.27 (eCFR, Title 31 up to date as of October 22, 2026, last amended October 15, 2026). Section 10.27(a) bars a practitioner from charging an unconscionable fee in connection with any matter before the IRS. Section 10.27(b) generally prohibits contingent fees for services rendered in connection with any matter before the IRS, with three exceptions: (1) services rendered in connection with the IRS's examination of, or challenge to, an original tax return, or an amended return or claim for refund or credit filed within 120 days of the taxpayer receiving a written notice of the examination of, or a written challenge to, the original return; (2) a claim for credit or refund filed solely in connection with the determination of statutory interest or penalties assessed by the IRS; and (3) services rendered in connection with any judicial proceeding arising under the Internal Revenue Code.

Important qualification: In Ridgely v. Lew, 55 F. Supp. 3d 89 (D.D.C. 2014), Civil Action No. 1:12-cv-00565 (CRC), signed July 16, 2014, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted summary judgment to Gerald Lee Ridgely, Jr., a practicing CPA, and permanently enjoined enforcement of the §10.27 contingent fee restrictions with respect to the preparation and filing of "ordinary refund claims," meaning refund claims filed after the original return but before the IRS has begun an examination. The court held that the IRS lacked statutory authority under 31 U.S.C. §330 to regulate that activity because preparing and filing such claims is not "practice" before the Treasury, and it rejected the argument that a CPA's status brings all of his conduct within Circular 230. Trade press reporting the decision (Journal of Accountancy and The Tax Adviser) dates it July 17, 2014, which appears to be the date of entry; the reported opinion is signed July 16, 2014. The IRS decided not to appeal, and the decision became final (Accounting Today, September 30, 2014). The text of §10.27 remains unchanged on the eCFR, so the regulation reads more broadly than it can currently be enforced.

Practical effect (analysis): Contingent fees remain lawful for many amended-return R&D refund claims filed before an examination begins, and §10.27(b)(2) separately permits contingent fees for work on an examination. Whether 30% is "too high" is therefore a pricing and risk question rather than a question of legality, subject to the general bar on unconscionable fees in §10.27(a) and to any state accountancy board or professional conduct rules that apply to the particular provider. Contingent fees for preparing an original return remain restricted.

Correction: Acena Consulting's guide states that firms may no longer charge a fee based on the percentage of savings for an R&D study, and describes hourly quotes capped at around 30% of the credit as a way to work within that restriction. Read alone, that overstates the current position in light of Ridgely. The guide is undated and appears to predate the decision.
4.3 Who bears the risk if a claim is examined

Brown Rudnick describes the reverse: a business that relied on professional advice may bring a professional negligence claim against the adviser. The briefing states that advisory firms generally owe a duty of care to their clients, and that this applies to unregulated "R&D boutiques" as well as to qualified accountants and tax professionals. Where a business knowingly overstated its claim or turned a blind eye, a negligence claim is much harder to bring; most cases involve businesses that relied on advice in good faith. This is a UK legal analysis.
The Brown Rudnick briefing states that over the last decade a growing number of firms, often outside the mainstream accountancy and legal sectors, began offering R&D tax credit services.

The source cited (J. David Tax Law, October 20, 2025) states that hiring a tax attorney in New York typically costs $350 to $800 per hour, adding that top attorneys in Manhattan sometimes charge over $1,000. The over-$1,000 figure is the top end, not the typical range, and the source covers New York only.

Two sources point the same way: Acena Consulting treats audit defense as an add-on that is priced separately or bundled at an added cost of 15% to 100%, and Hull & Knarr says a company may have to pay an additional fee to have the provider defend its work.
5. The fixed-fee alternative

A business comparing a 30% fee with a fixed fee should compare the actual written engagement terms for audit support on both sides: who will represent the business in an examination, at what cost, at what level of appeal, and what happens to the fee if the credit is reduced. Under a 30% contingency arrangement, the fee may or may not be refunded if the IRS later reduces the credit, and that term is often more important to the real cost than the headline percentage.
6. Answer: is 30% too high?
Analysis, based on the facts above:

items: 30% is at the top of every published range found (UK and Canadian sources; the Canadian source tops out at 25%; no US survey of §41 contingency rates was located).
Because the fee scales with the credit, it can greatly exceed the $7,500 to $50,000 base cost range for documenting a US study, particularly on larger or well-documented claims (Scenarios A and C).
On small, complex claims, a percentage fee may be below the cost of the work (Scenario B), so the answer depends on claim size and complexity.

Commentary from US and UK practitioners links percentage fees to an incentive to over-claim. The credit's qualification rules (§41(d), including the internal use software exclusion in §41(d)(4)(E); Treas. Reg. §1.41-2 on general and administrative costs; Treas. Reg. §1.41-4 on the process of experimentation and the 80 percent "substantially all" rule) are what an inflated claim would fail in an examination, and the client bears the resulting tax, interest and any penalties.

Contingent fees for ordinary refund claims are not prohibited by Circular 230 after Ridgely v. Lew, 55 F. Supp. 3d 89 (D.D.C. 2014), and §10.27(b)(2) permits contingent fees for examination work, so a 30% fee is not unlawful as such; the question is value and risk, subject to the bar on unconscionable fees.
What the fee includes if the claim is examined is decisive.
